candidates.verbatim_text_span: What is risk analysis? • A stage in the risk management process where risks are rated according to the criteria established by the organization • The most common criteria used for risk rating are the probability/likelihood and the impact • Allows for risk profiling, using risk matrices • This allows managers to prioritize risks for the urgency and degree of treatment – Separate major risks from minor risks – See which risks need regular checks – Identify suitable risk responses and – Identify suitable risk reports and assurance 39

Artificial Key parts of AI is ability to perform tasks without supervision and to learn to improve intelligence performance Machine learning is a set of algorithms which by themselves learn to make decisions or to structure data. Machine Supervised and unsupervised learning are based on data, while reinforcement learning learning is where the algorithm uses trial and error to learn to make sequences of decisions. In addition, the course underlines the significance of comprehending the risk, impacts and threats posed by new developments in AI technology, as well as the application of present regulations. Ethical issues in AI, AI governance, AI system transformation, ethical risk assessment and management, ethical matrices, along with societal and educational AI ethics will be among the subjects covered. 2

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Case Study Question / Instruction (5%) Context choice: Select any domain (e.g., healthcare, ﬁnance, education, logistics, environment, or others) where an AI system could be developed or deployed. Scenario: AI systems are often given a proxy goal (X’) that is measurable, but it may not fully match the true human or organizational goal (X). This is known as the AI ethics alignment problem: the goals programmed into the AI do not fully reﬂect human values or intentions. Task (Group of 2- 3, Max 4 slides): 1. Context and Goal (1 Mark): Describe the context you have chosen and clearly state:  The true goal (X) of the human/company.  The proxy goal (X’) given to the AI. 2. Conﬂict (1 Mark): Explain a situation where the AI optimizing for X’ could conﬂict with achieving true goal, X. 3. Inner Alignment (1 Mark): Propose how you would ensure the AI’s training objective matches the proxy goal (X’) correctly. 4. Outer Alignment (1 Mark): Propose how you would ensure the proxy goal (X’) remains consistent with the true goal (X). 5. Reﬂection (0.5 Mark): Why is alignment critical for responsible and trustworthy AI in your chosen context? 6. Peer Perspectives (0.5 Mark): Present different/similar views (Item 3 and 4) of the 2–3 group members and explain how you reached a shared conclusion (e.g. The group concludes that inner alignment requires “xxx”, outer alignment requires “yyy”) Submission: Upload to e-learning by 17 Sept 2025.

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Why Responsible AI Matters Now? • Risks of irresponsible AI act (e.g., bias, misuse, lack of responsibility, accountability, transparency, explainability, privacy, data protection, autonomy and control ) • Rapid Digital Innovation: Technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and Big Data are reshaping every aspect of life. This Venn diagram shows how Ethics, Technology, and Society are deeply interconnected in the digital era. • The Technology circle represents innovations like AI, big data, and IoT. • The Ethics circle reminds us that these technologies must be guided by principles like fairness, accountability, and human rights. • The Society circle highlights the people and communities affected by technology how it shapes lives, opportunities, and risks. • AI that is technically robust, ethically sound, and socially responsible. If one circle is ignored say, technology is deployed without ethics we get outcomes like bias, privacy invasion, or loss of public trust. • New Ethical Dilemmas such as: Data Ownership: Who owns the data collected by AI? Informed Consent: Do users understand how their data is used? Algorithmic Bias: Are decisions fair and free from discrimination? Accountability: Who is responsible when AI makes a harmful decision?

AI Context Example: ➢Applying fairness constraints, data anonymization, or human- in-the-loop systems. ➢Example: Introducing explainability tools to help users understand how an AI model make decision. 3. Monitoring & Review Goal: Continuously track performance and ethical compliance post-deployment. candidates.verbatim_text_span: The AIGE : Seven (7) AI Principles The development of AI must be designed to avoid bias or discrimination against the target users. AI systems must not take a one-size-fits-all approach and needs to address the widest possible range of factors (e.g. age, gender, religion, and ethnicity). FAIRNESS This enables equitable access and 3 1 PRIVACY AND SECURITY the active participation of all stakeholders. AI systems should be safe and secure, and perform as intended, and resist being compromised by unauthorised parties. Developers should where necessary obtain consent from individuals before using or disclosing personal data for AI development and deployment. The systems must guarantee privacy and data protection throughout the entire life cycle of the AI system. Information and data collected from users must not be used in an unlawful or discriminatory way against them. Developers also should incorporate security-by-design and privacy-by-design principles and refer to international standards related to information security and privacy when implementing the AI system. AI systems or solutions must be robustly tested to be reliable, safe and fail-safe by default so that users can trust and depend on the AI solution. To ensure proper access, control and protection of critical situations, AI systems should work reliably, consistently and operate in a real world under normal circumstances and unexpected conditions. In order to prevent or mitigate negative outcomes, AI systems must be able to response quickly according to the intended purposes. Developers and end-users are encouraged to carry out relevant testing and certification as well as risk and impact assessments to prevent any potential harm and mitigate risks. Autonomous systems must have safeguards to ensure ultimate controllability by humans, particularly when it comes to the applications of AI in high-risk areas such as autonomous vehicles, military applications, and when human life is at stake. 2 RELIABILITY, SAFETY AND CONTROL https://mastic.mosti.gov.my/publication/the-national-guidelines-on-ai-governance-ethics/

Scenario: AI systems are often given a proxy goal (X’) that is measurable, but it may not fully match the true human or organizational goal (X). This is known as the AI ethics alignment problem: the goals programmed into the AI do not fully reﬂect human values or intentions. Task (Group of 2- 3, Max 4 slides): 1. Context and Goal (1 Mark): Describe the context you have chosen and clearly state:  The true goal (X) of the human/company.  The proxy goal (X’) given to the AI. 2. Conﬂict (1 Mark): Explain a situation where the AI optimizing for X’ could conﬂict with achieving true goal, X. 3. Inner Alignment (1 Mark): Propose how you would ensure the AI’s training objective matches the proxy goal (X’) correctly. 4. Outer Alignment (1 Mark): Propose how you would ensure the proxy goal (X’) remains consistent with the true goal (X). 5. Reﬂection (0.5 Mark): Why is alignment critical for responsible and trustworthy AI in your chosen context? 6. Peer Perspectives (0.5 Mark): Present different/similar views (Item 3 and 4) of the 2–3 group members and explain how you reached a shared conclusion (e.g. The group concludes that inner alignment requires “xxx”, outer alignment requires “yyy”) Submission: Upload to e-learning by 17 Sept 2025.

candidates.verbatim_text_span: RAI Practice in Implementation Stage: RAI Governance via APIs (1) To restrict the way AI systems are used, developers can provide AI services in the cloud and control the interactions with these services via APIs. Context: Some AI systems may possess high-risk capabilities, which can be used or modified to perform harmful tasks. These capabilities may include natural language processing, speech and facial recognition, and decision-making abilities. It is crucial for developers to be aware of these high-risk capabilities and implement strict access controls to prevent any suspicious activity. Problem: How can developers limit the use of AI systems? Solution: To prevent harmful dual use, developers should anticipate misuse, enforce usage restrictions, and manage AI access through secure APIs or cloud platforms. Benefit: RAI governance via APIs supports regulatory compliance and protects against malicious use by controlling access and preventing unauthorized modifications Drawback: RAI governance via APIs can cause cloud provider dependence, limit user access, and reduce performance compared to local deployment 17

Because the ethical performance of AI models may degrade over time,
candidates.verbatim_text_span: RAI Practice in Operation Stage: Continuous Deployment for RAI New AI system versions can be deployed seamlessly using strategies that ensure RAI compliance  Context: AI systems are often required to evolve frequently due to their dependence on data. Because the ethical performance of AI models may degrade over time, they need to be retrained with new data or features and reintegrated into the AI components. The non-AI components may also need to be upgraded. As a result, it is necessary to continuously and frequently deploy new versions of AI systems into production environments. However, the autonomy of AI systems introduces a higher degree of uncertainty and risk.  Problem: How can we ensure that new versions of AI systems are seamlessly deployed to production environments? Solution: Deployment strategies like phased rollout, A/B testing, and redundancy help ensure seamless AI deployment while managing ethical risks and performance Benefit: Continuous deployment reduces ethical risks by enabling early detection and improves customer satisfaction through faster delivery of ethically sound AI models. Drawback: Continuous deployment can increase system complexity and make monitoring more challenging. 22

candidates.verbatim_text_span: RAI Practice in Operation Stage: Continuous Deployment for RAI New AI system versions can be deployed seamlessly using strategies that ensure RAI compliance  Context: AI systems are often required to evolve frequently due to their dependence on data. Because the ethical performance of AI models may degrade over time, they need to be retrained with new data or features and reintegrated into the AI components. The non-AI components may also need to be upgraded. As a result, it is necessary to continuously and frequently deploy new versions of AI systems into production environments. However, the autonomy of AI systems introduces a higher degree of uncertainty and risk.  Problem: How can we ensure that new versions of AI systems are seamlessly deployed to production environments? Solution: Deployment strategies like phased rollout, A/B testing, and redundancy help ensure seamless AI deployment while managing ethical risks and performance Benefit: Continuous deployment reduces ethical risks by enabling early detection and improves customer satisfaction through faster delivery of ethically sound AI models. Drawback: Continuous deployment can increase system complexity and make monitoring more challenging. 22

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Introduction • Clustering or cluster analysis is a machine learning technique, which groups the unlabelled dataset. It can be defined as "A way of grouping the data points into different clusters, consisting of similar data points. The objects with the possible similarities remain in a group that has less or no similarities with another group.“ • It does it by finding some similar patterns in the unlabelled dataset such as shape, size, color, behavior, etc., and divides them as per the presence and absence of those similar patterns. • It is an unsupervised learning method; hence no supervision is provided to the algorithm, and it deals with the unlabeled dataset. • After applying this clustering technique, each cluster or group is provided with a cluster-ID. ML system can use this id to simplify the processing of large and complex datasets. • The clustering technique is commonly used for statistical data analysis. UTM UNVERSITTEKNOLOGIMALAYSIA

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Cross validation Cross validation is a model assessment technique used to evaluate a machine learning algorithm’s performance in making predictions on new datasets that it has not been trained on. This is done by partitioning the known dataset, using a subset to train the algorithm and the remaining data for testing. Each round of cross-validation involves randomly partitioning the original dataset into a training set and a testing set. The training set is then used to train a supervised learning algorithm and the testing set is used to evaluate its performance. This process is repeated several times and the average cross-validation error is used as a performance indicator. https://www.mathworks.com/discovery/cross-validation.html UTM Faculty of Artificial Intelligsence UNIVERSITTEKNOLOGI MALAYSIA

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Detecting Overfitting and Underfitting In real-life scenarios when data is not in two-dimensional, visualizing the data and the cluster centres might not help us to detect overfitting or underfitting. We also may not have the access to the true cluster labels. Generally, in unsupervised learning, overfitting and underfitting are more difficult to quantify than in supervised learning due to several reasons: ●Performance may depend on our intuition and require human evaluation. ●If we know the true labels, we can measure the accuracy of the clustering. But we do not have the labels for unsupervised learning. If our model is probabilistic, in order to detect overfitting without labels is to compare the log- likelihood between the training set and a holdout set. Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture8-unsupervised-learning.html#the-language-of-unsupervised-learning UTM Faculty of Artificial Intelligence UNIVERSITITEKNOLOGIMALAYSIA

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Common terms in AI world (recap)… Overall term describing a set of different kinds of techniques and technology to make machines and computers behave in some kind of intelligent fashion. candidates.verbatim_text_span: The AIGE : Seven (7) AI Principles The development of AI must be designed to avoid bias or discrimination against the target users. AI systems must not take a one-size-fits-all approach and needs to address the widest possible range of factors (e.g. age, gender, religion, and ethnicity). FAIRNESS This enables equitable access and 3 1 PRIVACY AND SECURITY the active participation of all stakeholders. AI systems should be safe and secure, and perform as intended, and resist being compromised by unauthorised parties. Developers should where necessary obtain consent from individuals before using or disclosing personal data for AI development and deployment. The systems must guarantee privacy and data protection throughout the entire life cycle of the AI system. Information and data collected from users must not be used in an unlawful or discriminatory way against them. Developers also should incorporate security-by-design and privacy-by-design principles and refer to international standards related to information security and privacy when implementing the AI system. AI systems or solutions must be robustly tested to be reliable, safe and fail-safe by default so that users can trust and depend on the AI solution. To ensure proper access, control and protection of critical situations, AI systems should work reliably, consistently and operate in a real world under normal circumstances and unexpected conditions. In order to prevent or mitigate negative outcomes, AI systems must be able to response quickly according to the intended purposes. Developers and end-users are encouraged to carry out relevant testing and certification as well as risk and impact assessments to prevent any potential harm and mitigate risks. Autonomous systems must have safeguards to ensure ultimate controllability by humans, particularly when it comes to the applications of AI in high-risk areas such as autonomous vehicles, military applications, and when human life is at stake. 2 RELIABILITY, SAFETY AND CONTROL https://mastic.mosti.gov.my/publication/the-national-guidelines-on-ai-governance-ethics/

candidates.verbatim_text_span: ESTABLISHMENT OF AI GOVERNANCE SYSTEM Act / Regulation Ensure that your AI governance system aligns with existing legal frameworks and regulations. Address issues related to the 7 principles that may apply to AI applications in your jurisdiction. Technical & Ethics Standards Refine a set of 7 AI principles that will serve as the foundation for your policy. The standard should align with the 7 principles and the policy expectations. Establishing an AI governance system involves developing a structured framework that guides the ethical, legal, and responsible use of artificial intelligence technologies within your value chain. Coordination Clearly define roles and responsibilities for all stakeholders involved in the AI life cycle. Specify who is accountable for ethical considerations, compliance with policies, and oversight of AI projects that relate to the policy. By establishing your own AI Governance System related to your policy, you will gain a thorough understanding of AI technologies, their potential applications, and the ethical considerations associated with their use. This will also help you to develop a more comprehensive policy that details how AI technologies should be developed, deployed, and used within your value chain and include specific guidelines on data handling, algorithmic decision-making, transparency, bias mitigation, and accountability. Control Implement oversight mechanisms to ensure that AI systems adhere to established policies and ethical principles. This may involve regular audits, reviews, and assessments of AI projects to identify and address any ethical or legal concerns. However, keep in mind that the governance system needs to implement a feedback loop and mechanisms for continuous improvement. Regularly reassess and adapt your AI governance system based on the evolving landscape of AI technologies, emerging ethical considerations, and lessons learned from previous projects. Monitoring Integrate monitoring and evaluation processes into the AI governance system. Establish key performance indicators (KPIs) and metrics to assess the performance, impact, and ethical implications of AI systems throughout their life cycle. https://ai.gov.my/governance https://jpkn.sabah.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/THE-NATIONAL-GUIDELINES- ON-AI-GOVERNANCE-ETHICS.pdf AIGovernanceSystem Act/Regulation Technical&Ethics

It is crucial for developers to be aware of these high-risk capabilities and implement strict access controls to prevent any suspicious activity. Problem: How can developers limit the use of AI systems? Solution: To prevent harmful dual use, developers should anticipate misuse, enforce usage restrictions, and manage AI access through secure APIs or cloud platforms. Benefit: RAI governance via APIs supports regulatory compliance and protects against malicious use by controlling access and preventing unauthorized modifications Drawback: RAI governance via APIs can cause cloud provider dependence, limit user access, and reduce performance compared to local deployment 17

candidates.verbatim_text_span: RAI Practice in Operation Stage: Continuous Deployment for RAI New AI system versions can be deployed seamlessly using strategies that ensure RAI compliance  Context: AI systems are often required to evolve frequently due to their dependence on data. Because the ethical performance of AI models may degrade over time, they need to be retrained with new data or features and reintegrated into the AI components. The non-AI components may also need to be upgraded. As a result, it is necessary to continuously and frequently deploy new versions of AI systems into production environments. However, the autonomy of AI systems introduces a higher degree of uncertainty and risk.  Problem: How can we ensure that new versions of AI systems are seamlessly deployed to production environments? Solution: Deployment strategies like phased rollout, A/B testing, and redundancy help ensure seamless AI deployment while managing ethical risks and performance Benefit: Continuous deployment reduces ethical risks by enabling early detection and improves customer satisfaction through faster delivery of ethically sound AI models. Drawback: Continuous deployment can increase system complexity and make monitoring more challenging. 22

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Cross validation Cross validation is a model assessment technique used to evaluate a machine learning algorithm’s performance in making predictions on new datasets that it has not been trained on. This is done by partitioning the known dataset, using a subset to train the algorithm and the remaining data for testing. Each round of cross-validation involves randomly partitioning the original dataset into a training set and a testing set. The training set is then used to train a supervised learning algorithm and the testing set is used to evaluate its performance. This process is repeated several times and the average cross-validation error is used as a performance indicator. https://www.mathworks.com/discovery/cross-validation.html UTM Faculty of Artificial Intelligsence UNIVERSITTEKNOLOGI MALAYSIA

candidates.verbatim_text_span: Detecting Overfitting and Underfitting In real-life scenarios when data is not in two-dimensional, visualizing the data and the cluster centres might not help us to detect overfitting or underfitting. We also may not have the access to the true cluster labels. Generally, in unsupervised learning, overfitting and underfitting are more difficult to quantify than in supervised learning due to several reasons: ●Performance may depend on our intuition and require human evaluation. ●If we know the true labels, we can measure the accuracy of the clustering. But we do not have the labels for unsupervised learning. If our model is probabilistic, in order to detect overfitting without labels is to compare the log- likelihood between the training set and a holdout set. Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture8-unsupervised-learning.html#the-language-of-unsupervised-learning UTM Faculty of Artificial Intelligence UNIVERSITITEKNOLOGIMALAYSIA
